comparator.sourceNotes: Official current-student pages establish a 180-EC programme with 75 EC compulsory, 60 EC major choice and 45 EC profiling space. The compulsory part consists of six 7.5-EC first-year foundations and methods courses plus the four-stage 30-EC Bachelor Project (ethnographic methods, research design, fieldwork and thesis). Eight 7.5-EC major electives are required. No formal specialisation is imposed; the first eight electives in current official display order are instantiated neutrally, while the six-course profiling space remains open.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The broad closest match covers cultural anthropology's theory, comparative society and qualitative-research identity. Two direct programme-interest clusters support substantially distinct routes in migration/identity/inequality and globalisation/community change. Each contains a feasible 24-course schedule and production stops at the maximum of three alternatives.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both introduce comparative study of culture, society and social organisation.
Both develop theoretical analysis of social ordering and meaning.
Both engage advanced histories and theories used to interpret contemporary societies.
The comparator's philosophical anthropology elective has no sufficiently direct UCR counterpart.
Both examine gender as a historically and socially constructed relation.
Both examine how language choices produce meaning and identity; the comparator adds ethnography and sociolinguistic theory.
No UCR course in the selected union directly reproduces the anthropology of lived religion, media and popular culture.
The comparator's dedicated scientific-writing elective remains unmatched rather than being equated with a broader communication course.
The comparator's specific anthropological study of dominant norms in organisations has no single direct UCR counterpart.
Both examine transnational structures and global interdependence; the comparator grounds these in everyday sociocultural complexity.
Both examine violence, security and conflict; the comparator emphasises situated ethnographic perspectives.
The comparator's dedicated policy-and-evaluation research course has no sufficiently direct selected UCR equivalent.
Both introduce empirical social research, with UCR specialising in qualitative methodology.
Both develop an advanced research design and a sustained scholarly project, although the comparator prepares ethnographic fieldwork.
The comparator's applied mixed methods and statistics component remains unmatched.
The comparator's dedicated ethnographic field-methods course has no full UCR equivalent.
The comparator requires supervised ethnographic fieldwork that UCR does not reproduce.
The comparator thesis integrates its fieldwork results; UCR's standardized optional independent research element is displayed alongside it.
The six-course profiling space remains open and is not treated as fixed anthropology content.

notes.text: Utrecht combines a prescribed anthropology core with eight major electives and a compulsory 30-EC ethnographic Bachelor Project including fieldwork and thesis. UCR can construct strong culture-and-society pathways with qualitative research, identity, power and global-change content, but it does not reproduce the dedicated ethnographic fieldwork sequence; shared rows indicate substantive overlap rather than full equivalence.
